title: http (package)
objectives: Understand the http package via a real-life analogy
Send GET / POST / multipart requests correctly
Use MockClient / IOClient / BaseClient for testing + interception
Handle timeouts, cancellation, streaming, retries manually
Know when to graduate from http to Dio / Retrofit

sections.markdown:
**Think of `package:http` as walking to the post office yourself.**

You hand-address every envelope, you buy the stamps at the counter, you carry it back if the address is wrong. No sorting facility, no FedEx truck, no automatic retries.

- **Perfect for** — a card to your grandmother once a month (one endpoint, no cross-cutting concerns, tiny app).
- **Fine for** — a library that runs anywhere Dart runs (server, CLI, Flutter, Web) without pulling in Dio's IO layer.
- **Painful for** — a serious mobile app with auth, retry, logging, cancel-on-dispose. You end up writing a mini-Dio inside your BaseClient. At that point just use Dio.

**The Dart team maintains `http` as the *portable* HTTP primitive.** It's small, cross-platform (browser + IO), and every other client (Dio, Retrofit, gRPC-web) ultimately sits on top of similar plumbing. Knowing `http` well means you understand what higher-level clients abstract away — timeouts, connection pooling, MIME encoding, streaming.

**`package:http`** is the Dart team's official, portable HTTP client. Ships a functional API (`http.get / post / put / delete`), a `Client` class with connection reuse, `MultipartRequest` for uploads, streamed responses via `send()`, pluggable `BaseClient` for interception, and `MockClient` for tests. **Runs on** VM (dart:io) + Web (BrowserClient with `dart:html`) + WASM. **Does NOT include** interceptors, retries, cancellation tokens, or upload progress — you build those on top.

## Common mistakes

**Mistake 1: Not reusing a Client.** Every call to `http.get()` opens + tears down a new HttpClient — no connection reuse, one extra TCP + TLS handshake per request. Use a shared `http.Client()` and `close()` on dispose.
**Mistake 2: No timeout.** `http.get` waits forever if the server never responds. Always `.timeout(Duration(seconds: N))`.
**Mistake 3: `response.body` for JSON without validating status.** 500 with an HTML error page = `jsonDecode` throws. Check `statusCode` first.
**Mistake 4: Forgetting to `close()` a Client.** Sockets leak → 'Too many open files' on cellular flakiness.
**Mistake 5: Rebuilding a `MultipartRequest` for retry.** File streams are one-shot; you must re-open on retry. This is a reason people migrate to Dio.
**Mistake 6: Logging entire body in production.** PII + tokens in logcat. Gate with `kDebugMode`.
**Mistake 7: Building your own retry loop without idempotency guard.** Retrying POST duplicates orders.
**Mistake 8: Ignoring redirects.** `http` follows 3xx by default up to 5 hops; for OAuth flows you sometimes want to observe the redirect. Set `followRedirects: false` on a `Request`.
## Best practices
**1. Shared Client** — one long-lived `http.Client` per API host; close on scope exit.
**2. Always timeout** — connect / total via `Future.timeout`.
**3. BaseClient subclass** for auth / logging / retry across all calls.
**4. Typed responses** — decode inside a `Repository` / `ApiClient`, not at call sites.
**5. MockClient in tests** — no network.
**6. Retry idempotent methods only** — GET / PUT / DELETE, or use `Idempotency-Key` on POST.
**7. Buffer request bodies before retry** — streams are one-shot.
**8. Graduate to Dio** when the BaseClient starts to grow beyond ~150 lines.
## Practice programs
**Practice 1 (Easy)** — GET + JSON decode with status + timeout handling.
**Practice 2 (Easy)** — Shared Client; close in `dispose`.
**Practice 3 (Medium)** — BaseClient adds Bearer + logs latency.
**Practice 4 (Medium)** — MultipartRequest with re-openable file stream.
**Practice 5 (Hard)** — Retry-with-backoff BaseClient + idempotency guard.
**Practice 6 (Hard)** — MockClient test that exercises 401 refresh + retry through your BaseClient.
**Practice 7 (Expert)** — Migrate the same app to Dio; measure LOC saved + latency change from connection reuse.
## Interview Q&A

**Q1: When would you pick `http` over Dio?**

**A:** Three clear cases. **(1) A pure-Dart library** you publish to pub.dev — Dio pulls Flutter engine deps; `http` runs on VM + Web + WASM + server, so a networking library that must be portable stays on `http`. **(2) Prototypes / one-endpoint apps** — the interceptor machinery is overkill. **(3) Server-side Dart** (Shelf, backend services) — Dio is designed for client apps. **In production Flutter apps** with real auth, retry, logging, cancellation needs — Dio wins because you don't hand-roll the same 200 lines of BaseClient every project. Interviewers score highly on 'they know when to pick the small tool.'

**Q2: What's the difference between the functional `http.get()` and a `Client()`?**

**A:** `http.get()` and friends are **convenience shorthands** that internally construct a new `Client`, make the call, and close it. Fine for one-off calls. But **each call opens a fresh TCP + TLS handshake** — no connection reuse. On mobile cellular, that's 200-500 ms extra per request. **A long-lived `http.Client()`** reuses sockets (Keep-Alive by default in `dart:io`'s `HttpClient` — the underlying implementation). One handshake, N requests. Rule: any screen making > 1 request per interaction should hold a shared `Client`, and every app should hold one at the DI-container level. **Always `.close()`** when scope exits — otherwise sockets leak and eventually you hit 'too many open files' on flaky networks.

**Q3: How do you implement request cancellation with the `http` package?**

**A:** `http` has **no CancelToken**. Two workarounds: **(1) Screen-scoped Client** — hold an `http.Client()` per screen, call `.close()` in `dispose`. Any in-flight request throws `ClientException`. Coarse — you cancel all requests on that client together. **(2) Explicit `Request` + streamed cancel** — for individual requests, wrap in a `Completer` and race with a manual 'cancelled' flag; on cancel, ignore the response. **(3) `Future.timeout`** — cancels at a deadline. **The truth:** none of these are as clean as Dio's `CancelToken`. If cancellation matters (list refresh, search-as-you-type), migrate to Dio. Also always check `mounted` before `setState` on the resolved future — cancellation is racy without proper tokens.

**Q4: How do BaseClient subclasses replace interceptors?**

**A:** `http` has no interceptor chain, but you can `extend http.BaseClient` and override `send(BaseRequest)`. Every `get / post / put` internally calls `send`, so your subclass sees every request. **Pattern:** attach auth header, log, retry, refresh on 401, all in the override; delegate the actual network call to an inner `Client`. **Limitations vs Dio interceptors:** (1) no chain composition — you write one monolithic `send`. (2) `BaseRequest` bodies are streams; **cloning for retry requires you to buffer `bodyBytes` yourself**, and streamed requests can't be replayed at all. (3) no per-request skip mechanism (Dio has `RequestOptions.extra`). At about the point where your `BaseClient` grows past 150-200 lines, you're re-implementing Dio poorly — switch.

**Q5: How do you test code that uses the `http` package?**

**A:** Use `MockClient` from `package:http/testing.dart`. Takes a callback `(Request) => Future<Response>`; returns canned responses per URL / method. Inject the client via constructor into your `ApiClient`; in tests, construct with `MockClient`. **Advantages:** in-memory, deterministic, no `HttpOverrides` global hack. **Also test:** timeout handling (mock delays with `Future.delayed`), non-200 responses, JSON parse errors. **Don't test the underlying network** — it's slow, flaky, and someone else's job. For integration tests hitting a real staging environment, use a **local mock server** (Wiremock, `shelf`-based fake) instead of hammering staging.

**Q6: When should you graduate from `http` to Dio, and how do you migrate?**

**A:** Graduate when: **(1)** BaseClient has both auth AND retry AND logging — clearly reinventing an interceptor chain. **(2)** Any screen needs cancel-on-dispose (which is any screen with search / infinite scroll / editable filters). **(3)** Multipart uploads with progress bars — `http` requires you to manually track byte counts. **(4)** > 3 API hosts with different auth. **Migration recipe:** (1) create a Dio instance in DI; (2) rewrite `ApiClient.get/post` methods one-for-one — response API is very similar; (3) replace `Future.timeout` with `BaseOptions.receiveTimeout`; (4) replace BaseClient logic with Dio interceptors (one commit per concern — auth, retry, log); (5) delete BaseClient. Usually ~1 day for a mid-size app; net LOC goes down.

## Real-world usage

- **Dart packages published to pub.dev** — GitHub OAuth libs, weather API wrappers, tiny SDKs.
- **Server-side Dart** — Shelf handlers, CLI tools.
- **Prototypes / hack-week projects** — one endpoint, no cross-cutting concerns.
- **Under the hood** — Firebase Dart SDK, `googleapis`, and many other libs use `http` for portability.
- **NOT ideal for** — production Flutter apps with auth+retry+logging needs (use Dio).

## Advanced notes

- **`IOClient`** — wraps a `dart:io HttpClient` for advanced socket / TLS config (badCertificateCallback, custom user agent).
- **`BrowserClient`** — used automatically on Web; supports CORS + credentials.
- **`RetryClient`** — from `package:http/retry.dart` — small pre-built retry wrapper with backoff.
- **`http_client_helper`** — 3rd-party CancelToken layer if you must stay on `http`.
- **`StreamedRequest`** — for outbound streaming (WebSocket handshake, chunk upload).
- **`followRedirects: false`** on a Request when you need to observe 3xx (OAuth PKCE).
- **Cookie management** is manual on IO — set `Cookie` header yourself; use `dart:io HttpClient` directly for jar semantics.
- **HTTPS pinning** — subclass IOClient + custom `SecurityContext.setTrustedCertificatesBytes`.
- **Web platform quirks** — no user-agent control, no arbitrary headers on cross-origin without preflight — plan for CORS.
- **`http` 1.x** shipped a stricter `Uri.parse` that rejects invalid URIs earlier; migrate error handling for `FormatException` at Uri creation.
